comments.author: @millennialfalcon1547
comments.text: People always make the mistake of thinking that technology scales exponentially or even at the same rate. This isn't true. Technology is logarithmic. It's biggest gains are in the very beginning and then its rate of increase slows over time and flattens out. This means that the big returns on compute have already happened. That's why they have moved to RL (reinforcement learning). Soon those gains will start to diminish as well. What usually keeps a technology going is the fact that very smart people continue to make new breakthroughs in techniques and algorithms and hardware and software. It's like one logarithmic curve leads to the next then the next then the next. This gives the overall appearance that the technology is increasing at a steady rate upwards. But without new technique breakthroughs beyond RL the AI curve will start to flatten. Open AI knows this too. That's why they need 10x what Grok is doing now just to get probably a 30% increase in overall capability.

comments.author: @JohannesVinter
comments.text:
You can’t directly compare GPUs and TPUs since they’re optimized for different things, but the usual metrics are FLOPS (at FP16/BF16/FP8), memory bandwidth, power efficiency, and cost per training run.
Nvidia H100 GPU → ~2 PFLOPS (FP8), ~3 TB/s bandwidth, very flexible and supported everywhere (PyTorch, TF, etc.).
Google TPU v4 → ~275 TFLOPS (BF16), ~4.8 TB/s bandwidth, great for large-scale training but more locked to XLA/JAX/TF.
AWS Trainium → ~190 TFLOPS (BF16/FP16), optimized for price/performance in training, but smaller ecosystem.
👉 In practice, people compare them by how fast and how cheap they can train the same model. GPUs win on flexibility + ecosystem, TPUs/Trainium can win on efficiency and cost at scale.
